edges.effect_quant: In an RCT of 75 non-dialysis CKD patients with iron-deficiency anemia, intravenous iron produced greater Kidney Disease Quality of Life improvement than oral iron; an updated meta-analysis of 24 CKD trials found intravenous iron increased the chance of achieving a hemoglobin rise greater than 1 g/dL (RR 1.61, 95% CI 1.39-1.87 for CKD stages 3-5), a plausible pathway for better fatigue and function.
edges.population: adults with chronic kidney disease and iron deficiency with or without anemia treated with intravenous iron
edges.mechanism: Intravenous iron bypasses poor gut absorption and can replete iron stores more rapidly than oral therapy in CKD. Faster restoration of ferritin, transferrin saturation, and hemoglobin can reduce fatigue and activity limitation, although patient-reported benefits are not uniform across all CKD subgroups.
edges.summary: Intravenous iron often improves iron indices and sometimes quality-of-life measures in CKD-related chronic anemia, but the patient-reported benefit is mixed rather than universal. The overall direction leans favorable, especially when oral iron is poorly tolerated or insufficient, but the effect size on day-to-day functioning appears modest.
edges.caveats: Not every randomized trial shows a clear quality-of-life gain, and some CKD trials were small or short. Intravenous iron also carries tradeoffs including infusion burden, hypotension risk, and in some studies more serious adverse events than oral iron.
